steps.text: **What the lesson asks.** You will be able to say how a prepared line trades a wrecked pawn structure for active pieces, and why that can be fair. At each decision ask three things: what does the structure invite, what is forced, and which piece has the most to do? Then compare with the engine and the game.

**Black spends time to gain space.** In the Meran, Black takes a pawn on c4 and plays a pawn to b5 to chase the bishop, so Black's queenside pawns advance while White builds a centre. Both sides are betting: White on the central pawns, Black on the squares the advanced pawns will open. Watch for the bet as you step through.

steps.text: **Why a break.** White's pawns on d4 and e4 stand side by side and hold the centre. A pawn that attacks a pawn from the side is a *break*: it can trade a defender off or open lines. [I] Here ...c5 hits d4, so White has to decide: defend it, push past it, or let it go for activity. At depth 16 e5 and d5 are both close to the best.

steps.text: **Preparation is not magic.** The knight on f6 gave White a target: the pawn on e5 could capture it. steps.text: **What the sacrifice did.** The knight went to e6 and was taken, then the rook took the knight on d7: knight for knight. Rooks came off, and the g3 pawn took Black's bishop on f4. After 24.gxf4 White has five pawns to three, with queen, rook and bishop each, yet the engine at depth 16 reads the position as about level. Black's active pieces are paying for the damaged pawns; the later moves test whether that holds. [I]

steps.text: **Two turning points.** 29.Ra3 was a slip: at depth 16 it is at least 0.6 pawns below Rd1. 33.Bd3 was the collapse: at least eight pawns below the best move, and from there Black wins the queen. A game is often lost at a late blunder, but a quiet slip can make it possible. [I] Both numbers are engine evidence, not proof.

**Teach it back.** Imagine a beginner who asks why a sacrifice needs a target. In your own words give the idea, one position where it works, one where it fails, and one warning. Use the two knight positions from the contrast step if you like. Then check yourself against the list on the next card. The app does not grade it.

**Self-check.** Did you say when it works (a target exists, a file opens, a piece is defended)? When it fails (nothing to capture)? Is your example one a beginner could set up? Did you name a mistake? Compare your move-13 choice: at depth 16 castling is at least 0.3 pawns better than the capture. **Remember:** a damaged pawn structure is a price, not a verdict; count what you get for it. A forcing move needs a target. Check who defends the landing square.
